e-595.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Parametric Curve
e-595.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\cos{t}, \quad y=\sin{t}, \qquad  0\leq t<2\pi,
$$

 calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14077511/assets/2ec95dd061fa6b7f09c9f899a1f6483b4ea7d5127372ddd6eefb74d6ed10c14c.png)
e-595.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = -\sin{t}, \qquad y'(t)=\cos{t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t} = -\cot t.
$$

e-596.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
e-596.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
e-596.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t + te^t = (1+t)e^t, \qquad y'(t)=-e^{-t}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-{e}^{-t}}{(1+t){e}^{t}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1+t){e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2(1)}(1+1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=({t}^{3}-1){e}^{t},\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=0.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=({t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-1){e}^{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{({t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-1){e}^{t}}.
$$

At the point where $t=0$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{({0}^{3}+3\cdot {0}^{2}-1){e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{2(1)}{(-1)\cdot 1} \\  & =-2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=2t{e}^{t},\,y={t}^{2}+2t,\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{t}(t+1),\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t+2.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t+2}{2{e}^{t}(t+1)}=\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve 

$$
x={t}^{5}-2t,\,y=1-{t}^{3},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=-1.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}-2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-3{t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-3{t}^{2}}{5{t}^{4}-2}.
$$

At the point where $t=-1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-3(-1)^{2}}{5(-1)^{4}-2} \\  & =\frac{-3}{5-2} \\  & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,

after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /6} & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve 

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

shown above, calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /6} & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
